note: Blind grouping: produced from blind_classes.json only. Ordered by shape (root cause), largest groups first, singletons last.

groups.label: one mutable object behind two names
groups.why: A container is built once and referenced from two owners (a shared row list, one list for every dict key, a class attribute, a def-time default, a one-level copy), so a mutation through one name is visible through the other.

groups.label: documented error branch missing; the underlying call's exception escapes
groups.why: The docstring names what happens on the bad input (None, a default, a project exception) and the code has no branch that achieves it, so the built-in raises its own ValueError/TypeError/JSONDecodeError/ZeroDivisionError instead.

groups.label: truthiness stands in for the documented presence test
groups.why: A filter or `x or default` uses Python truthiness where the doc promises a None/emptiness test, so 0, '', [], False and None are all conflated.

groups.label: caller's own object mutated or handed back as the result
groups.why: The docstring promises a new independent object and the code mutates the argument in place and/or returns the same object it was given.

groups.label: predicate built from a weaker primitive than the claim
groups.why: The test used is strictly weaker than the documented relation - substring for word, reference identity for content equality, equality to one empty type for emptiness, syntax check without the reserved-word check.

groups.label: last, partial or unterminated piece of the sequence mishandled
groups.why: The loop bound or divisor is derived from the nominal size instead of handling the tail, so a final partial window, chunk, batch or the remainder of a zip is dropped or mis-averaged.

groups.label: documented failure never happens; a silently wrong value is returned
groups.why: The docstring promises a raise (or a specific sentinel) on failure and the code returns an ordinary value instead, so the caller sees success.

groups.label: output order is not the documented order
groups.why: The docstring claims a specific output order (input order preserved, ascending numeric) and the container/insertion/comparator used imposes a different one.

groups.label: newline/line-terminator model differs from the claim
groups.why: Lines are counted or split with a delimiter primitive whose treatment of the final terminator contradicts the docstring's model (a final unterminated line counts, keepends, a trailing newline makes no empty last line).

groups.label: str.strip used as affix removal (argument is a character set)
groups.why: The code calls strip/rstrip to remove a prefix, suffix or leading slash, but those arguments are character sets, so any of those characters is eaten at either end.

groups.label: strict inequality where the documented rule is inclusive
groups.why: A strict < guards a comparison whose documented meaning includes the equal/touching case, so equal neighbours and touching intervals are treated as outside.

groups.label: search returns a match, not the documented first match
groups.why: The loop reports whichever occurrence it happened to hit (the midpoint, or the last one because it never breaks) while the docstring promises the index of the first occurrence.

groups.label: implementation assumes its input is already ordered or grouped
groups.why: Both rely on the sequence arriving in order - one takes the last element as the maximum, the other removes only adjacent equal elements - and the docstring claims the general unsorted case.

groups.label: loop bookkeeping goes stale when the structure changes during the pass
groups.why: The state the loop tests against (the shifting index, the once-built seen set) is not updated as elements are removed or appended, so elements in the batch are skipped or duplicated.

groups.label: state computed once by a lazy/consuming/eager-short-circuit construct
groups.why: The docstring assumes a full pass over the data, but the iterator is single-use and all() stops at the first failure, so the second pass and the later records never happen.

groups.label: a documented length bound applied to only one part of the result
groups.why: The bound in the docstring covers the whole result, while the slice (of n, or of max_len) is applied to the payload alone, so a longer input is truncated or the suffix pushes the result past the bound.

groups.label: string method's count/limit argument not what the docstring says
groups.why: str.split and str.replace are called without the maxsplit/count that the docstring's 'first occurrence only' or 'every occurrence' requires, so the operation runs over the wrong number of matches.

groups.label: true division used where floor division was documented
groups.why: The code divides with / (or int(a / b)), which yields a float or truncates toward zero, while the docstring describes floor semantics that // gives.

groups.label: bool/int interchangeability defeats the type test
groups.why: Because bool is a subclass of int and 0 == False, an isinstance test counts booleans and set membership collapses 0/False and 1/True, which the docstring assumes are distinct values.

groups.label: only half of a two-part normalisation performed
groups.why: The docstring promises two normalisations (case and punctuation, key and value) and the code applies exactly one of them, leaving the promised-ignored part in place.

groups.label: capitalise/title built-in also lowercases the rest
groups.why: The docstring promises that only the first letter changes, but the built-in used (title, capitalize) lowercases every following character - and title also splits on apostrophes.

groups.label: empty argument special-cased to the opposite of the docstring
groups.why: An explicit `if not needle/prefix` branch returns -1 or False for the empty string, exactly inverting the documented result (found at the end, matches everything).

groups.label: out-of-range argument not normalised although the docstring names it
groups.why: The docstring spells out the case where the argument exceeds the data (negative n, k larger than the list) and the code feeds it straight into a slice, so the documented wrapping/empty result never happens.

groups.label: greedy regex spans from the first to the last delimiter
groups.why: A single unbounded quantifier makes the pattern eat everything between the first '<' and the last '>', deleting content along with the tags.

groups.label: wrong library mode discards data instead of substituting
groups.why: encode('ascii', 'ignore') drops the offending character where the docstring promises a replacement character.

groups.label: a representation detail of the input leaks into the predicate
groups.why: The sign kept by the string form makes a negative number fail a palindromic test the docstring claims it passes.

groups.label: numeric tie rule of the primitive differs from the documented rule
groups.why: round() resolves exact halves to even while the docstring promises halves away from zero.

groups.label: no-match branch yields the input itself
groups.why: With no dot to split on, the last field is the whole basename, so the missing case returns the input instead of the documented empty string.

groups.label: one nesting level handled where the docstring claims arbitrary depth
groups.why: The comprehension removes exactly one level of nesting, so deeper lists survive the flatten.

groups.label: one branch of a standard algorithm diverges from its definition
groups.why: The even-length branch of the median returns a middle element instead of the mean of the two middle elements.

groups.label: advertised default is actually the opt-in flag
groups.why: The parameter that implements the documented default behaviour defaults to False, so the docstring's default behaviour requires an explicit opt-in.

groups.label: unit threshold and unit divisor disagree
groups.why: The code switches unit at 1000 (SI) while dividing by 1024 (binary), so the value printed for the boundary input follows neither system the docstring claims.

groups.label: collision precedence opposite to the docstring
groups.why: The docstring says the first mapping wins and dict.update lets the later one overwrite it.

groups.label: closure binds the loop variable at call time
groups.why: Every lambda looks up i when it is called, so all of them see the final value instead of the value from their own iteration.

groups.label: fixed index slicing instead of the documented token boundary
groups.why: The text is cut at a character index rather than at the word boundary the docstring promises, so words and spaces are split mid-token.

unclear.why: i078 is a copy that is one level too shallow and i028 is a flatten that handles one level of nesting; I put i078 with the shared-object group because its probe demonstrates two names on one object, but the depth reading would pair it with i028.
The aliasing split (mutating the caller's own object vs. one object shared among owners) is a judgement call; i057 returns the argument itself, which could belong to either.
Both are failures of the documented return/raise protocol: I separated 'the library's exception escapes' from 'a wrong value is returned silently', but a single probe template could catch both.
i037 divides a last partial batch by the nominal size and i043 applies a length bound to one component; both are 'the limit is computed from the wrong quantity', so either grouping is defensible.
Both are about claims of uniqueness, but i003's root cause is order destroyed by set()+sort while i059's is a seen-set built once; I could not decide whether the author sees one shape or two.
The two JavaScript items could be one class ('a JS built-in default is not the documented semantics'), but i021 sits in my ordering group and i051 in the weaker-predicate group.

i033's implementing flag defaults to False and i035's fill parameter is never read; both are 'the advertised parameter does not do what the docstring says', but i035 is read more naturally as the last-chunk case.

i023's sign is kept where the palindromic rule should ignore it and i022's punctuation is kept where the docstring says it is ignored; that is the same normalisation complaint, but i023's docstring never names the sign.
Both return a wrong value in the not-found case (the input itself, None instead of -1); one is a string-slicing accident and the other an except-clause choice.
Both are documented handling of a degenerate argument (out-of-range, empty) that the code implements as its opposite; the mechanisms differ (slice semantics vs an explicit early return).
Exhausting an iterator and mutating a list during iteration are both 'the pass does not see the elements it should', but one is library laziness and the other an index shift, so I kept them apart.
